Datum DNS: resource model, conditions, and provenance

This is orientation, not a procedure. When a customer's question matches a
known failure shape, load the matching skill instead of reasoning from this
document alone — it tells you what things mean, not what to check first.

## The resource model

Everything lives under the API group dns.networking.miloapis.com/v1alpha1,
in four kinds:

- DNSZone: a customer's domain. spec.domainName is immutable once set.
- DNSRecordSet: records grouped by zone and by DNS record type (A, AAAA,
  CNAME, TXT, and so on). One DNSRecordSet holds one or more owner names,
  and each owner name inside it is tracked and reported on independently.
- DNSZoneClass: cluster-scoped. Names the controller and the nameserver
  policy a zone is provisioned under. Customers do not create these.
- DNSZoneDiscovery: a one-shot snapshot of what a domain currently
  resolves to, used when importing an existing zone that was managed
  elsewhere before.

The fact worth holding onto: a record set is not a record. A DNSRecordSet
named "www-a" might hold only "www", or it might hold "www", "app", and
"@" together, each with its own status. Ownership is tracked per (zone,
record type, owner name), not per DNSRecordSet object.

## Reading conditions: the taxonomy

Every DNSZone and DNSRecordSet reports an Accepted condition (admission)
and a Programmed condition (whether it is live in the DNS backend).
Reasons on Programmed fall into a few buckets:

- Self-clearing, no customer action needed: Pending,
  PendingDomainVerification (but see below — this one still needs the
  customer to act on a different object).
- Needs a person to act, and never clears by itself: NotOwner, Conflict,
  DNSZoneInUse.
- Depends on the message: PDNSError. The same reason covers a value the
  customer typed wrong, a zone still coming up, and a backend hiccup —
  read the message, don't stop at the reason code.
- Anything else you don't recognize: treat it as needing attention rather
  than assuming it's healthy. An unrecognized reason is far more likely to
  be a new failure than a new success.

The single most important thing to get right: Pending is the absence of a
cause, not a promise of progress. A record waiting on a zone that never
finishes provisioning is Pending forever, and reading it as "still working
normally" after an hour is a wrong answer that sounds confident. Healthy
only within a bounded window — the diagnose tools already carry that
window and tell you when a wait has gone on too long.

## Where the real status lives

For a DNSRecordSet, the answer to "is this record live" is
status.recordSets[], one entry per owner name, never the top-level
Programmed condition. That top-level condition is a rollup: it names only
the first blocked name in sorted order, plus "and N more" if there are
others. Reading it alone hides everything but the alphabetically first
problem.

Owner names must be compared qualified and case-folded before you decide
two entries refer to the same thing. The backend treats "www",
"WWW.example.com", and "www.example.com." as identical, but a record set
can carry status for more than one spelling of the same name at once, and
those entries can disagree — one saying Programmed, the other saying
Conflict. The diagnose tools already do this matching for you; don't
compare owner-name strings yourself.

## Record types and the surprises

Fourteen record types are supported: A, AAAA, ALIAS, CNAME, TXT, MX, SRV,
CAA, NS, SOA, PTR, TLSA, HTTPS, SVCB. A few behaviors are easy to miss:

- CNAME and ALIAS are single-valued. Extra values submitted alongside one
  are silently dropped, not rejected.
- TXT content is quoted and semicolons are escaped automatically.
- SOA's serial number defaults to a date-stamped value if not set.
- TTL defaults to 300 seconds when the customer doesn't set one. Nothing
  enforces a minimum or maximum TTL anywhere in the system.

## The owner-name spelling trap

This is a live, documented sharp edge, not a hypothetical. When a record
is created, ownership of a name is decided by comparing spellings exactly
as typed — "www" and "WWW" are different as far as that decision is
concerned — but the backend itself keys everything on the fully qualified,
case-folded name. So it's possible for two different spellings of the
same name to both "win" their own ownership check, both write to the same
underlying record at the DNS backend, and neither ever reports NotOwner —
whichever wrote most recently silently wins, and the other looks fine in
its own status while serving nothing.

If a customer describes a record that "looks right but serves the old
value," or a record that seems fine in one place and broken in another,
suspect two spellings of one name before anything else. The guidance is
simple: pick one spelling per name and use it consistently.

One more edge on this: a name written as a full, absolute FQDN is taken at
face value and is not checked against the zone it's attached to. Sending
an out-of-zone FQDN reaches the DNS backend, which then rejects it with an
"outside the zone" style message.

## Provenance: who actually owns a record

Not every DNSRecordSet is created by the customer. Three other producers
write them, and editing one that belongs to a controller doesn't stick —
the controller reverts it:

- The AI Edge (Datum's Gateway DNS integration) creates and manages
  records that route traffic through it. These carry a small set of
  labels marking them as controller-owned.
- The iroh connector writes TXT records for its own endpoint verification.
- An external-dns integration can also manage records here, marked with
  its own label.
- The zone's own SOA and apex NS records are created by Datum itself and
  carry no labels at all — they're recognized by their shape (record
  type and owner name), not a marker.

When a customer wants to edit something and it's controller-managed, the
right answer names which controller owns it and points them at editing
the source object, not this record.

## Delegation and verification: separate from programming

A zone being "Programmed" only means Datum finished writing its own
default records. It says nothing about whether the domain's registrar has
actually pointed at Datum's nameservers. Those are two independent facts:
- The nameservers Datum assigned live on the zone's own status.
- What the registrar has actually published is a separate, observed
  value, and it can simply be unknown if nobody has checked yet — unknown
  is not the same as "not delegated," and reporting it that way sends a
  customer to blame their registrar for a check that never ran.

Domain ownership verification is a different, earlier gate entirely, on a
separate Domain object. Until a domain passes verification, nothing about
its DNS zone gets provisioned at all, no matter what the zone's own
conditions say.

## DNSSEC is not supported

This is severe enough to say plainly, not as a footnote: if a domain has
DNSSEC turned on at the registrar, or has old DS records still cached at
the parent, delegating it to Datum's nameservers without disabling DNSSEC
first will make it stop resolving for anyone using a validating resolver
— and that failure can look completely healthy from every angle available
here.

## What this assistant cannot see

Be honest about the edges: resolver-side caching behavior, anything about
the customer's registrar account itself, and DNS propagation beyond what
a live query happens to report at the moment you ask. Say so rather than
guessing at answers that depend on data outside this system.
